summary:
ARES-NAV is an interactive, web-based decision-support and navigation interface engineered for future human surface excursions on Mars, specifically targeting the Arsia Mons volcanic region.
To bridge the gap between global orbital datasets and specific astronaut needs, we integrated multi-layered NASA Mars Trek WMTS data—combining MOLA elevation, THEMIS Day/Night thermal infrared, and Viking optical mosaics—with surface radiation metrics, verified lava tube skylights, and a Gemini AI mission advisor.
This unified tool directly addresses the challenge of ensuring astronaut safety and mission efficiency during Marswalks. By synthesizing four distinct environmental data types into an instant Habitat Suitability Score and a slope-aware Rover Traverse Planner (flagging hazardous inclines over 15°), ARES-NAV enables explorers to safely navigate rough basaltic terrain, minimize radiation exposure, and target high-value geological sites like subsurface lava tubes.
Ultimately, ARES-NAV transforms complex, fragmented planetary science into real-time, actionable intelligence. By providing real-time hazard alerts and environmental scoring directly on the surface, ARES-NAV minimizes EVA risks and allows crews to focus on high-priority geological sampling.
details:
Project Overview: What ARES-NAV Does & How It WorksARES-NAV (Arsia Mons Decision-Support) is an interactive, web-based planetary mission-planning and survival navigation platform designed for human and robotic exploration of Mars. Focused on the volcanic flank of Arsia Mons in the Tharsis region, ARES-NAV solves one of the primary barriers to long-term human presence on Mars: identifying safe, accessible subsurface radiation shelters while plotting survivable surface traverse routes.

Users interact with a real-time mission control interface built directly on top of NASA Mars Trek Web Map Tile Service (WMTS) datasets. By layering topographic, thermal, and optical orbital maps with adjustable opacity, mission planners can click any coordinate on Arsia Mons to generate an instant Habitat Suitability Score (0–100). The platform evaluates elevation, slope gradient, surface thermal inertia (distinguishing load-bearing basaltic bedrock from hazardous loose dust), proximity to verified Arsia Mons lava tube skylights, and estimated annual ionizing radiation exposure (mSv/yr). Additionally, ARES-NAV features an integrated Rover Traverse Planner that computes point-to-point (A → B) distances using Mars's true planetary radius (R = 3,389.5 km), estimates Small Exploration Vehicle (SEV) travel durations, and generates an elevation profile that flags dangerous slopes exceeding 15° in red. An embedded AI Mission Advisor (powered by the Google Gemini Flash API) further synthesizes these telemetry metrics into tactical exploration directives.

Key Benefits

Multi-Spectral Data Fusion in One Interface: Eliminates the need to switch between separate GIS tools by blending MOLA elevation, THEMIS Day/Night Infrared, and Viking Color mosaics with real-time transparency controls.

Quantitative Site Selection: Converts complex planetary science parameters (thermal inertia in SIU, slope angles, radiation dosage, and skylight proximity) into an actionable, graded Habitat Suitability Score.

Traverse Risk Mitigation: Prevents rover or crewed vehicle immobilization by automatically detecting steep terrain (>15°) along planned routes before deployment.

Zero-Installation Accessibility: Runs natively in any modern web browser without requiring heavy desktop GIS software or specialized hardware.

Intended Impact

ARES-NAV bridges the gap between raw NASA orbital reconnaissance data and practical surface mission operations. For future human missions to Mars, deep volcanic lava tubes offer natural shielding against galactic cosmic rays (GCRs), solar particle events (SPEs), micrometeorites, and extreme diurnal temperature swings. By pinpointing verified skylights near navigable terrain, ARES-NAV demonstrates how future astronauts and autonomous rovers could locate and reach subterranean habitats safely. Beyond mission-planning utility, the platform serves as an educational decision-support simulator that allows students, researchers, and space enthusiasts to experience real planetary engineering trade-offs firsthand.

Tools, Coding Languages, Data Sources & Software Used

Orbital Datasets: NASA Mars Trek WMTS APIs — Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) Elevation, Mars Odyssey THEMIS Day & Night Infrared (IR) thermal imagery, and Viking Color Mosaic.

Frontend & Core Logic: HTML5, CSS3, and modern JavaScript (ES6+) for geospatial coordinate math, planetary great-circle distance calculations (R = 3,389.5 km), elevation profiling, and dynamic UI telemetry.

AI Integration: Google Gemini Flash API (with user-configurable API key support) for context-aware mission analysis and site recommendations.

Deployment & Hosting: Netlify cloud hosting for continuous deployment and global web access.

How ARES-NAV Is Creative

Rather than presenting Mars as a static map or a simple educational encyclopedia, ARES-NAV transforms planetary cartography into a live Mission Control decision-support console. Its creativity lies in combining four distinct disciplines into a single cohesive workflow:

Planetary Geology (using THEMIS Night IR thermal inertia to separate solid basalt from rover-trapping dust),

Radiation Protection Engineering (anchoring habitat scores around verified lava tube skylights),

Autonomous Navigation Physics (calculating SEV traverse times and slope thresholds across realistic Martian curvature), and

Generative AI (embedding an interactive mission advisor directly into the telemetry loop).

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

Radiation vs. Accessibility Trade-Off: High-altitude regions on Arsia Mons experience higher atmospheric radiation exposure (~282 mSv/yr), making immediate proximity to deep lava tube skylights critical for crew survival.

Surface Load-Bearing Capacity (Thermal Inertia): High elevation alone is insufficient if a landing or traverse zone is covered in thick, fine dust. We incorporated THEMIS thermal metrics (SIU) to prioritize exposed basaltic terrain capable of supporting heavy landers and rovers.

Rover Mobility & Slope Limits: Steep volcanic flanks and crater rims pose severe rollover and traction risks. Our traverse engine enforces a strict 15° slope warning threshold aligned with planetary rover engineering constraints.

True Planetary Geometry: All distance and scale calculations were calibrated specifically to Mars's mean radius (3,389.5 km) rather than Earth-based web map defaults, ensuring scientific accuracy.

As a result, through a division of labor and teamwork within our group, we have prepared this website and the presentation you are currently reviewing.
